title: Judging old histories and how the quarrel over Alexander and Arius and Constantine began
english: Philostorgius says he does not know who wrote the books of Maccabees, whoever it was. He approves the first book, since it agrees with the prophecies of Daniel. It also recounts very thoughtfully how the wickedness of men drove Jewish affairs to the depth of evils, and how the courage of men raised them again. Then they won back power over their enemies, and the temple was cleansed from Greek defilements. He says the second book shows a different writer, for it is an abridgment of the five volumes written by Jason of Cyrene. That work recounts the war which Judas Maccabeus waged against Antiochus Epiphanes and his son surnamed Eupator. He rejects the third book, calling it monstrous and wholly unlike the first. He too agrees that Josephus wrote the fourth, but he says it is less a history than a speech of praise, telling the story of Eleazar and the seven Maccabean children.

Philostorgius says Josephus differs from this Phlegon only in treating the events that befell the Jews at greater length, although Phlegon and Dion mentioned them only briefly and made them a parenthesis in their own narrative. For he shows no concern at all for matters that lead to piety and the rest of virtue, and they showed none either. Josephus, on the contrary, seems both fearful and cautious, lest he offend the Greeks.

Philostorgius praises Eusebius, the associate of Pamphilus, in everything else that belongs to history, but he says he went wrong concerning piety. This impious man explains the fault by saying that he held the divine to be unknown and incomprehensible, and that he committed other such errors. He adds that Eusebius closed the record of his history at the succession of the sons of Constantine the Great.

This impious man says the votes for the bishopric were falling to Arius, yet Arius preferred Alexander to himself and contrived to bring them round to him. Philostorgius speaks of a certain presbyter named Alexander Baucalis, so nicknamed because the mass of his overgrown flesh heaped on his upper back took the shape of an earthen jar, which people of the country commonly call baukala. He says this man held second rank and made the beginning of the cause from which the quarrel between Alexander the bishop and Arius broke out. The proclamation of same substance was contrived from that beginning.

Philostorgius says Constantius, the father of Constantine the Great, was appointed emperor over Upper Galatia for his valor, the land in which the so-called Alps lie. Those places are hard to invade and hard to enter, and men today call the Galatias the Gallias. The death of Constantius occurred in the land called Albion. His son Constantine found him sick there, after unexpectedly escaping the plot of Diocletian, and he buried him at his death and became successor to the emperorship.

Philostorgius agrees with the other writers that the change of Constantine the Great from Greek religion to Christianity came about through his victory over Daxentius. He records that victory as the cause.
